_comment: Interview question bank for the SDE job: 12 questions, three per competency.
Two uses. (1) Load into the real database via POST /questionLib/createOrUpdate so real
sessions have enough variety for non-overlapping subsets - the live bank has only 2
questions today, which is not enough for a meaningful golden set. (2) Source of truth for
the synthetic golden set in make_synthetic_golden.py.
reference_answer is what the grader compares against and is NOT NULL in the schema. It is
written as marking guidance rather than a model answer, because a grader handed a polished
essay tends to penalise every valid answer that took a different route.
aiSrc: reuse one avatar clip across all questions. The question text is overlaid on screen,
so there is no need to record 12 videos. Replace the placeholder with a real MinIO URL

questions.question: Something breaks in production and users are affected. Walk me through what you personally do, from the moment you find out.
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: confirming impact and scope before acting; checking recent changes (deploys, config, flags); a bias toward mitigation before root cause; use of concrete signals (logs, metrics, alerts) rather than guessing; communication to others; and a follow-up such as a postmortem or a new alert. Strong answers show they have felt the pressure of it - hesitation about rolling back, or a specific incident. Weak answers list tools without an order of operations.

questions.question: How do you approach designing a system that needs to scale?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: asking what scale actually means here (reads vs writes, traffic shape, latency and consistency needs) before designing; statelessness and horizontal scaling; where state goes; caching with an explicit staleness tolerance; partitioning; failure handling; observability from the start. Strong answers name tradeoffs rather than technologies. Weak answers are a list of buzzwords - 'microservices, caching, load balancer' - with no reasoning about which problem each solves.

questions.question: You are reviewing a teammate's pull request and you think the approach is wrong - not a small bug, the whole design. How do you handle it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: separating the observation from the judgement; asking about constraints they may know and the reviewer does not; moving out of the PR comments for a design disagreement; concrete alternatives rather than 'this is wrong'; awareness of cost - how far along they are, whether it is reversible. Strong answers mention they have been wrong doing this before. Weak answers are either conflict-avoidant ('I'd just approve it') or purely technical with no attention to the person.

questions.question: A query that used to be fast is now taking eight seconds. Where do you start?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: measuring before changing - EXPLAIN or the query plan; asking what changed (data volume, a new column, a code change, statistics); understanding whether an index is missing, unused, or newly unhelpful; awareness that adding indexes has a write cost; checking whether the query is actually the problem or the symptom (lock contention, N+1 from the caller). Strong answers distinguish 'slow for everyone' from 'slow for this one tenant whose data grew'.

questions.question: You are designing an API endpoint that other teams will call. What decisions matter most?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: the contract as the hard-to-change part; naming and resource modelling; pagination for anything list-shaped; error semantics and what the caller can do about each error; idempotency for writes; versioning and how it will be deprecated; auth. Strong answers think about the caller's failure modes, not just the happy path, and mention that you cannot un-ship a field. Weak answers are REST-verb trivia.

questions.question: How do you decide what to test, when there is never time to test everything?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: risk-based reasoning - what breaks silently, what is expensive to get wrong, what changes often; the distinction between tests that catch regressions and tests that pin down current behaviour; skepticism about coverage as a target; tests as documentation. Strong answers describe something they chose NOT to test and why. Weak answers recite the test pyramid without applying it.

questions.question: Two requests arrive at the same time and both try to update the same record. What can go wrong, and what would you do about it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: naming lost update or a read-modify-write race; a concrete mechanism - optimistic locking with a version column, a transaction with the right isolation level, a conditional update, or a queue; awareness that the right answer depends on contention and on whether losing an update is actually harmful. Strong answers ask what the business consequence of a lost update is before choosing. Weak answers say 'use a lock' with no further detail.

questions.question: Explain something technical you have worked on to someone who is smart but not an engineer.
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: starting from why it mattered rather than how it worked; an analogy that does not collapse under a follow-up question; avoiding jargon without becoming vague; checking for understanding. Strong answers pick something genuinely complex rather than something easy to explain. Weak answers either stay technical or become so simplified that nothing is conveyed.

questions.question: Tell me about a technical decision you made where you were choosing between two reasonable options.
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: both options stated fairly - the rejected one should sound genuinely viable; the criteria used to decide; constraints (time, team, existing system); what they would revisit now. Strong answers name what the decision cost them, since real tradeoffs have a downside. Weak answers describe an obviously correct choice dressed up as a dilemma.

questions.question: Tell me about the hardest bug you have had to track down. What made it hard?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: an actual method - narrowing the search space, forming and testing hypotheses, bisecting, reproducing reliably; what made it hard (intermittent, cross-system, environment-specific, misleading symptoms); what they changed afterwards to prevent a repeat. Strong answers include the wrong hypothesis they chased first. Weak answers are 'it was a typo' or a story with no visible reasoning.

questions.question: You need to change a piece of code that is old, important, and has no tests. How do you go about it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: characterisation tests pinning current behaviour before changing it; small reversible steps; finding out why it is the way it is before assuming it is bad; a rollback plan; verifying in production. Strong answers show respect for code that has survived - the odd branch is often load-bearing. Weak answers jump straight to rewriting it.

questions.question: Describe a time you disagreed with a decision your team made. What did you do?
questions.referenceAnswer: Look for: making the case once, clearly, with reasoning rather than repetition; genuinely engaging with the other view; committing to the decision once made; knowing when a disagreement is worth escalating. Strong answers include an instance where they turned out to be wrong, or where they committed to something they still disagreed with. Weak answers are either 'I was right and eventually they saw it' or complete deference.
